label: Curvature
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 88 through 109 of do Carmo and asks how a Riemannian manifold bends. We motivate the curvature tensor as the precise obstruction to flatness, then trace it through sectional, Ricci, and scalar invariants that summarize bending at increasing levels of coarseness.

label: Failure to Commute
notes: On Euclidean space mixed second derivatives commute, so transporting along two orders agrees. On a curved manifold the covariant analogue fails, and the gap is exactly the curvature operator. We define R by this commutator and stress that the bracket term repairs the failure for non-coordinate fields.

label: The Curvature Tensor
notes: We confirm that the commutator definition is tensorial: R of X, Y acting on Z is linear over smooth functions in all three slots, so its value at a point depends only on the vectors there. This pointwise character is what lets curvature be read off a single tangent space.

label: Holonomy Around a Loop
notes: Parallel transporting a vector around a small coordinate loop returns it rotated, not unchanged. The infinitesimal rotation per unit area is the curvature operator. This holonomy picture is the geometric heart of the chapter and the one students should carry away from the algebra of the commutator.

label: Symmetries of R
notes: The curvature tensor obeys three algebraic symmetries: antisymmetry in the first pair, antisymmetry in the last pair, and pair-interchange symmetry. Together with the first Bianchi identity these cut the number of independent components dramatically and underlie every later trace and contraction we form.

label: The Bianchi Identity
notes: The first Bianchi identity is the cyclic sum of R over its first three arguments vanishing. It is an algebraic constraint following from the symmetry of the Levi-Civita connection, and it is indispensable when proving that sectional curvature determines the full tensor.

label: Sectional Curvature
notes: Sectional curvature assigns a number to each tangent two-plane by evaluating R on an orthonormal basis of that plane. The denominator normalizes for non-orthonormal spanning vectors. This single function of two-planes is the most geometric curvature invariant and generalizes the Gauss curvature of surfaces.

label: Sphere, Plane, Saddle
notes: Positive sectional curvature makes nearby geodesics converge as on a sphere; zero curvature keeps them parallel as in the plane; negative curvature makes them spread as on a saddle. This trichotomy is the visual signature of the sign of K and the payoff of the whole construction.

label: K Determines R
notes: A theorem of the chapter states that if sectional curvature is known on every two-plane then the full curvature tensor is determined. The proof uses the algebraic symmetries and a polarization argument. Constant sectional curvature yields the explicit model expression for R.

label: Ricci Curvature
notes: Ricci curvature is the trace of the curvature operator in one slot: average the sectional curvatures of planes containing a fixed direction. It is a symmetric bilinear form measuring how volume of a thin geodesic cone deviates from the Euclidean reference along that direction.

label: Scalar Curvature
notes: Scalar curvature is the full trace of Ricci, a single number at each point averaging all sectional curvatures through it. It is the coarsest curvature invariant and controls the leading volume defect of small geodesic balls compared with Euclidean balls of equal radius.

label: The Hierarchy of Curvature
notes: We close by stacking the invariants: the full tensor R, its sectional refinement on two-planes, the Ricci trace on directions, and the scalar trace at points. Each step discards information for a coarser summary, and recognizing what survives each trace is the chapter's organizing idea.
